Ōpaheke Park in Papakura is a remarkable new green space that offers something for everyone, blending recreation, relaxation, and environmental innovation across its expansive 19-hectare site. As one of South Auckland’s largest recently developed parks, it’s quickly become a go-to destination for locals looking to enjoy the outdoors in a setting that feels both natural and well planned. The park features a mix of wide open lawns, long walking and cycling trails, wetlands, ponds, sculpted earth mounds, and boardwalks that wind through the landscape, creating a peaceful and scenic environment that encourages exploration. Families are especially drawn to the large pump track designed for young bikers and scooter riders, while dog owners appreciate the dedicated off-leash dog area. Fitness enthusiasts can make use of the outdoor exercise stations spaced along the paths, and nature lovers will enjoy spotting birds and native wildlife among the more than 50,000 trees and plants that have been thoughtfully planted throughout the space.

One of the park’s standout qualities is its built-in flood resilience. Designed to absorb and manage stormwater, Ōpaheke Park plays a crucial role in protecting surrounding neighbourhoods—particularly flood-prone areas like Red Hill—by acting as a natural water retention system during heavy rainfall. This innovative design not only adds to the park’s functionality but also reflects a commitment to sustainable urban development. While the core features of the park are already complete and open to the public, some facilities such as clubrooms, shaded seating areas, and additional toilets are still being added in future development stages. Even so, the park feels spacious, clean, and highly usable, with plenty of space to spread out whether you’re visiting alone, with family, or in a group.

Access to the park is convenient, with nearby parking and footpath connections for pedestrians and cyclists. It’s an ideal spot for everything from a quiet morning walk or a casual afternoon picnic to a full family outing. On sunny days, the park comes alive with locals walking their dogs, kids zipping around on bikes, and residents simply soaking up the open space. It’s a refreshing escape from the busyness of everyday life and a prime example of how urban parks can be both beautiful and practical. As more facilities are added over time, Ōpaheke Park is set to become not just a local favourite but a model for what future community parks should aspire to be—inviting, environmentally conscious, and designed with everyone in mind.

You must try this glamping place—it’s a hidden gem! If you want to take your family camping but don’t want to set up tents, this is the perfect option. It’s also a great spot for a quiet getaway around Auckland.

You can tell that the owner has taken great care of the place and has put a lot of thought into providing customers with an excellent experience. We booked two domes, both of which were very cozy and beautifully designed with different themes: one had a European feel, while the other was styled in a Bohemian looks. Both domes were well-equipped with air conditioning and a mini indoor theater for us to watch Netflix. Some of us chose not to watch a movie, so we asked the owners to set up a bonfire. We relaxed outside, chatting with friends, enjoying our snack platter and wine, while gazing at the stars!

Oh, and the showers...man! Each doom had it's own private shower and bathroom, and we didn’t expect the water pressure to be so fantastic, especially at a glamping site. We must have each showered for over 20 minutes, just enjoying the experience without any interruptions since everyone else was busy with other activities, haha.

For our stay, we opted for the simple breakfast add-on, which included fresh local ingredients to prepare our own big breakfast. The kitchen had everything we needed to make our food, and we enjoyed our coffee and tea on the porch while taking in the view. Of course, and took lots of photos at this beautiful place before we leave too.

Once we finished breakfast and checked out, we explored a few nearby places. We visited Hunua Falls, which was only a 20-minute trip away, and also the Lavender Farm!

Overall, it was definitely a five-star getaway experience. We highly recommend it and will certainly return in the future!

My last-minute stay at The Nomad was absolutely wonderful, the perfect retreat for anyone needing a peaceful escape from everyday life. My niece had an amazing time too. We’ll definitely be returning!

Hunua Falls Reserve is simply amazing! A short walk takes you to the breathtaking waterfall surrounded by lush native forest. The peaceful vibe, scenic trails, and picnic spots make it a perfect nature escape. Great for photos, light hikes, or just soaking in the beauty—definitely worth the visit!

Nice place to walk the forests or just have the time to sit down and watch the waterfall. Longer walking tracks that can take up to 3 hours are available. Toilets on site were well maintained and they even had a caravan serving food such as hot dogs, burgers, ice cream etc

Cossey-Massey Loop is an awesome walk if you’re keen to get moving and enjoy some nature at the same time. It’s a decent workout with a mix of climbs, bush tracks, and a waterfall or two along the way. Perfect for clearing your head and staying active!

This hike starts from the Hunua Falls car park.
You can either take the stairs up to the right or continue straight on to start with the suspension bridge and dam. In both cases, the tour is very pleasant and very well laid out. There's a lookout over the lake about halfway along. Allow between 2h30 and 2h45 to complete the loop

My favourite track to walk in Auckland. Full of climbs and descents through lush native bush. At 8.3km this can be completed in an easy 3hrs with a medium level of fitness. Good footwear, water, a raincoat, and a backpack are recommended as the weather can change quickly. Don't go out in your jandels. This track can be very busy on the weekends, best to go early before the crowds arrive.

Great track for hiking on hot days as most of the trail is under leaf cover. Lots of uphill hiking so make sure you're well rested and ready to go. It says it should only take 3 hours but takes about 3.5 hours realistically for a more leisurely walk with short breaks.

I would label this a moderately challenging hike but there are many people who run it for exercise.

Would only recommend for kiddos who can handle longer focus times.

The view from the top of the hills is a killer and the beach is a beautiful, massive black sand beach with lovely swimming water. An especially big shout out to Peter, the groundskeeper, who made our stay particularly lovely, he made us feel like we already lived there, offered us tips, a ride, and went out of his way to help me personally when I lost my manaia. Thank you Peter, you're the loveliest soul!

This small reserve on Honey Place in Weymouth is a lovely little hidden gem, especially for families with young children. Tucked away in a quiet suburban street, it offers a peaceful and safe environment where kids can play freely. The reserve features a basic but well-maintained play area, including swings, which are always a hit with younger children. There’s also plenty of grassy space for running around, kicking a ball, or just enjoying a picnic on a sunny day.

What makes this reserve great is its simplicity — it’s not crowded, there’s little traffic nearby, and the atmosphere is calm. It’s a nice alternative to larger parks when you’re just after a short outing or a quiet place for the kids to burn off some energy without the noise and busyness of bigger playgrounds.

That said, there’s definitely room for a few improvements that could make the space even more inviting. Adding more flowers or native plants would really brighten up the area and attract birds, bees, and butterflies — making it not just a fun place, but also an educational one for kids who love nature. A small garden or even a few flowering shrubs would go a long way. It would also be great to see a couple more seating options for parents or grandparents to relax while keeping an eye on the children, and maybe some extra shade for those hot summer days.

Overall, the reserve is a lovely little community space that serves its purpose well. With just a few thoughtful additions, it could become an even more vibrant and enjoyable spot for locals and families to visit regularly. Definitely worth stopping by if you’re in the area.

This small reserve has all the basics of a nice green space—trees, open grass, and a peaceful atmosphere—but unfortunately, that’s about it. While it’s a nice spot to walk through or let the dog have a quick run, there’s really nothing here to encourage people to stay and enjoy the area. There’s no playground, no seating, no picnic tables, no BBQs—just grass and trees.

For a community space, it feels like a missed opportunity. Families walking past have nothing to do here. Parents with young children would have to keep moving because there’s nothing for kids to play on. Even something as simple as a couple of swings, a slide, or a climbing frame would completely change the feel of this space and give children a reason to enjoy it.

The lack of seating is another issue. There aren’t any benches or shaded spots to sit and relax. Elderly residents or anyone wanting to stop for a moment of peace might find it disappointing. Adding a few benches under the trees would make a world of difference for people who just want to enjoy the fresh air.

There’s also no clear path or signage, which might make the space feel underdeveloped or forgotten. It wouldn’t take much to make it more inviting—maybe a paved path, a rubbish bin, and a simple sign letting people know it’s a public reserve.

Right now, the area feels more like an empty lot than a park or community space. It’s green and quiet, yes, but it’s not useful or family-friendly in its current state. With a few small improvements, this could become a much-loved local reserve. Hopefully, the council can consider investing a bit into turning this underutilized patch of land into something people of all ages can actually enjoy.

The Waimai Road beach access to Weymouth Beach is one of those hidden local spots that’s great if you know what to expect — but it’s definitely not perfect. First thing to note is that there are no proper steps or handrails to guide you down to the shoreline. Instead, you’ll find a grassy slope that looks harmless at first, but can get extremely slippery, especially after a bit of rain or early in the morning when there’s dew. It’s easy to lose your footing if you’re not paying attention, so take extra care — especially if you’ve got kids, elderly family, or if you’re carrying gear.

Once you do make it down, the beach itself is actually quite lovely. Weymouth Beach isn’t massive, but it has a calm, quiet vibe that makes it perfect for a peaceful stroll or just sitting by the water. It’s not really the kind of beach you go to for a full day of swimming and sunbathing, but it has a charm of its own. Locals often walk their dogs here or stop by for a bit of fresh air. On a clear day, the view across the water is pretty relaxing, and you’ll sometimes spot a few paddleboarders or kayakers further out.

There’s no real surf here — the water tends to stay fairly still, which is great for calm reflection but maybe not so exciting for active swimmers. You won’t find much in the way of facilities either, so bring what you need. It’s best for a short visit rather than a full beach day.

The access works if you’re after something quiet and don’t mind rougher terrain, but be warned — watch your step. A bit of caution goes a long way here.

This small park is a valuable green space in the neighbourhood and has great potential to be a real community hub. It’s surrounded by large, mature trees that offer plenty of shade, making it ideal for dog walkers, families, and anyone wanting a peaceful spot to relax.

One of the park’s biggest strengths is its location — it’s close to several schools and just a short walk from the local dairy. This makes it easily accessible for students and families, and a great place to stop by after school or while out running errands.

However, the park could benefit from a few upgrades. Installing swings or some basic playground equipment would go a long way in making the space more inviting for children. At the moment, there’s not much to keep young kids engaged.

There are also occasional issues with people dumping shopping trolleys in the area. A bit of extra maintenance or community signage might help discourage this behaviour.

With a few small improvements, this park could become an even more vibrant and well-used space for the whole community.

McLeod Road Beach access is a bit of a hidden gem, though it’s definitely showing its age. The entrance features a set of old concrete steps that have seen better days—still functional, but worn down over time. There’s also a wheelchair-accessible ramp, which is a great inclusion and makes the beach more welcoming for everyone. However, a word of caution: when it rains, both the steps and the path can get very slippery, so it’s worth taking extra care on wet days.

Once you get down to the beach, you’re rewarded with a peaceful and scenic stretch of coastline. It’s usually quiet and not too crowded, making it perfect for a walk, a moment of reflection, or just soaking in the fresh air. The natural beauty of the beach really stands out.

Unfortunately, what takes away from the experience is the careless dumping of rubbish around the access point. It’s sad to see old tyres, gas bottles, and broken boxes left behind by people who clearly don’t appreciate the environment. It not only spoils the look of the area but can also be harmful to wildlife and dangerous for visitors.

Overall, McLeod Road Beach is still a lovely spot, but it could really shine with a bit more care from both the public and the local council. A proper cleanup, better maintenance, and some signage about dumping could go a long way. Despite its flaws, it’s still worth visiting—just be sure to watch your step if it’s been raining!

This beach access spot has quickly become one of my favourites — not just for the convenience, but for the overall experience it offers. Right from the start, beautiful parking spots makes a big difference. It’s easy to find a spot even on busier days, which takes the stress out of planning a visit. Whether you’re staying for a full beach day or just popping by for a walk, not having to worry about parking fees is a huge plus.

The walk down to the beach is pleasant and well maintained, with a wide, clear path and plenty of benches along the way. These are perfect for taking a break, chatting with friends, or simply soaking up the scenery. It’s an especially nice touch for older visitors or families with kids who might want to rest before or after the walk.

One of the real highlights of this location is the stunning view of the harbour and the airport. You can watch planes taking off and landing in the distance, which adds a unique and surprisingly peaceful backdrop to the whole experience. The combination of natural beauty and urban movement is something you don’t often get at a beach — and it makes this spot feel special.

The area is also very dog-friendly, and it’s clear that local dog owners love bringing their pets here. Most dogs are on leads and well behaved, and it’s nice to see them enjoying the space just as much as the people.

However, one downside is the littering. Despite the bins provided, it’s disheartening to see some people dumping rubbish along the path or near the dunes. It really detracts from what’s otherwise a clean and peaceful environment. A few more signs encouraging people to keep the area tidy — or even some regular community clean-up days — would go a long way toward preserving the beauty of the space.

Overall, this beach access point is a real gem. With free parking, easy access, relaxing seating, gorgeous views of the harbour and airport, and a friendly dog-walking crowd, it ticks almost every box. If people could be a little more mindful about rubbish, it would be nearly perfect.

Laurie Gibbons Memorial Park in Weymouth is a primo spot for a day out, especially if you’re keen on rugby, bringing the doggo, or just need a place with easy parking.

The rugby fields are in great nick—perfect for a solid game with your mates or watching the local club in action. The park’s got a real community vibe, and the clubrooms have had a spruce-up, making it a top spot for both players and supporters.

Parking’s a breeze here. There’s a decent-sized car park off Gibbons Road, so you won’t be doing laps looking for a spot. Even when there’s a game on, finding a park is usually sweet as.

Got a furry mate? Dogs are welcome at the park, but make sure to keep them on a leash unless signs say otherwise. It’s a great place for a walk, and there’s plenty of space for them to stretch their legs.

All up, Laurie Gibbons Memorial Park is a top-notch place to hang out—whether you’re there for the rugby, taking the dog for a stroll, or just enjoying the open space with easy parking.

This makes the beach accessible to everyone, including people with mobility issues, parents with prams, and anyone who finds stairs challenging. The slope is smooth and well-maintained, making it safe and easy to use.

You can tell that the local council has put real thought into making Weymouth Beach welcoming and inclusive. Whether you’re going for a swim, a walk along the shore, or just to relax and enjoy the view, this shortcut makes the journey to the beach much more enjoyable. The area is also rich in birdlife, with ducks, seagulls, and other coastal birds commonly seen waddling about or swimming nearby, adding a natural charm to the setting. It’s not a large space, but it offers a surprising amount of enjoyment for such a simple setup—a great little place to pause, de-stress, and watch life go by.

Becker Drive Reserve is a quiet, tucked-away gem nestled between homes in a peaceful residential area. While small and simple, it serves as a valuable green space for the local community—especially for families with young children. The playground, though basic, is clean and functional, with enough equipment to keep little ones entertained. However, there’s definitely room for improvement. Adding more flowers or low-maintenance native plants would brighten the space and make it feel more welcoming. A splash of color through landscaping could transform the reserve into a place not just for play, but for relaxation. Seating is limited, so a few more benches—especially shaded ones—would make a big difference for parents, grandparents, or anyone wanting a quiet moment outdoors. Picnic tables could also encourage family outings or casual community gatherings. Other suggestions include installing a drinking fountain for warmer days, creating a small walking path for light exercise, and perhaps even adding a community notice board or a little free library to help build neighborhood connections. Soft lighting could also enhance safety and usability in the early evenings. Overall, Becker Drive Reserve is already a helpful space for nearby residents, and with a few thoughtful additions, it could become a much-loved community hub.

Cosseys Creek Dam was the first of a series of rolled earth water supply dams in Auckland's Hunua Ranges which was completed in 1955. Auckland’s third largest dam, and it holds 14% of the city’s water storage. Dam is 49m high at the crest from the foundation and has a crest length of 170 m. The 230m long diversion tunnel links to the valve tower and scour systems. Reservoir covers 119 ha when full with a storage capacity of 14.5 million m3. The dam was built using residual clays and rubbles from greywacke-argillite rock with a puddle clay core to seal water seepage.

It took 14 months to fill the reservoir after the completion of the construction and the first spill occurred on the 12 July 1956.

I went for a walk around Wiri Mountain (also called Matukutūruru) recently, and honestly, it was a somewhat interesting spot. It’s not super flashy or developed like some of the other maunga around Auckland, but there’s definitely something special about it. You can tell it has a lot of history – it used to be a proper volcanic cone before it got heavily quarried, so most of the original shape is gone. But even now, you can still see old Māori pā terraces and there’s a cool lava cave nearby that’s apparently the longest in Auckland, but could not find it.

The area feels quiet and a bit hidden, which I actually liked. There’s a small carpark, which is handy – nothing huge, but enough space if you’re just going for a quick look or a walk. What caught my eye was this old shack on the site. It’s pretty small and boarded up now, but there’s something kind of charming about it – like a little piece of local history just sitting there waiting to be restored.

You can see the beginnings of some work being done – I noticed areas where they’re planting native trees and doing some cleanup. It looks like the council or some local groups are slowly working on improving the place, which is awesome. With a bit more time and care, I reckon it could turn into a really lovely community space. It’s already a good place to stretch your legs, take in some views, and learn a bit about the local history.

It’s not your typical touristy spot – more like a quiet, underrated gem with a lot of cultural value. I’ll definitely be coming back to see how it develops.

Cenotaph Park in Manurewa, formally known as Te Pae Maumahara or the Manurewa War Memorial Park, is a peaceful and deeply significant space that has served the local community for over a century. It may not be the largest or most visually striking park in Auckland, but what it lacks in grandeur it more than makes up for in historical value and emotional weight. At its centre stands a granite obelisk, originally unveiled on 2 January 1921 to commemorate 26 local soldiers who lost their lives during the First World War. Since then, additional plaques and inscriptions have been added to honour those who served in later conflicts, turning the monument into a layered symbol of collective remembrance.

The park has long been a gathering point for memorial services, especially on ANZAC Day and Armistice Day. These events are heartfelt and well-attended, often involving school groups, local RSA members, veterans, and families who gather to lay wreaths and reflect on the sacrifices made. There’s something uniquely moving about these ceremonies being held in a suburban setting, far from the busier inner-city memorials. It reminds you that war affected people in every corner of the country, including quiet streets like those around Manurewa. On any regular day, however, the park is a calm, somewhat underused spot where people occasionally stop by to sit beneath the mature trees or walk past the monument on their way to the nearby shops, library, or train station.

The park has its strengths, including its central location, easy access from public transport, and a surrounding area that provides a mix of green space and urban amenities. However, there are areas where it falls short. The infrastructure is starting to show its age. Some original plaques have been removed or faded over time, and certain features like the brick pillars and entrance gates—installed in 1955—could use restoration. The paths are basic, lighting is limited, and there’s a noticeable lack of seating or interpretive panels that could help visitors, especially younger generations, understand the context of the memorial and the lives behind the names. It’s a park with deep historical roots, but it hasn’t been given the same level of upkeep or enhancement that other war memorial sites around Auckland have received.

That said, the spirit of the park still holds strong. Its simplicity is, in many ways, part of its charm. Unlike more manicured or commercialised public spaces, Cenotaph Park feels genuine—built for remembrance rather than decoration. You can walk past it and feel the weight of time, the lives lost, and the quiet strength of a community that still comes together each year to remember. If the council were to invest in improving the space with subtle enhancements like updated signage, restored plaques, seating, and better landscaping, it could transform into an even more meaningful site, one that honours both the past and the living.

Cenotaph Park might not catch your eye at first glance, but for those who take a moment to stop and reflect, it offers something powerful—a tangible link to history, a place to pause and remember, and a reminder that even in the suburbs, stories of sacrifice and service are deeply rooted.

Absolutely awe inspiring trek but you have to be brave for the climb down the hill (cliff) face. The track is accessed from the loop track. There’s a 15m walk to the top and then about 30-45 minutes going down. Coming back up is a vigorous climb but almost easier than going down and a similar timeframe. I’ve picked 4hrs because once you’re down you’ll want to hang around enjoying the space and caves.

It’s wise to go with someone who has done this before because you can go off track and end up with a steeper and more dangerous route down. The track is reasonably safe, even the bit where someone (I don’t know who but thank you for all the work over the years!) has put in ropes to make it easier.

The alternative route is around from the northern end of Karekare but you have to time it at neap tide and be back before the tide comes in or else it’s a climb out.

At the bottom not only is there a beautiful secluded beach but there are caves. And you can swim through them!

At the northern end of the main beach is a cave that’s just a sliver in the cliff but it goes through to another little bay (it gets very dark so once again, you can be brave or take a torch). To the right as you come out is another cave that widens out into a tomo (collapsed clifftop or chimney). I call it the cathedral.

To the left is a cave with a dead end. When the tide is not fully out you can swim through it which is cool.

In addition, you can walk around the point back to the main beach (or swim if the tide is not fully low) and there’s a bridge formed where the cliff has fallen in at both ends and the water has scooped out a swimming pool! There’s even a rock that you can jump off into the pool. It’s absolutely magical.

Both are sandy floor and I’ve seen a stingray swimming in the bay quite close to shore but haven’t encountered anything any other time I’ve been there, so figure we make enough noise to scare them off.

We explored the Puhinui Stream Walkway in Wiri, Auckland, on Christmas Day 2024, and it was a remarkable experience. The absence of other visitors provided a serene and tranquil atmosphere, allowing us to fully immerse ourselves in the unique urban landscape.

The walkway meanders alongside the Puhinui Stream, which flows through an industrial area. The juxtaposition of the natural stream against the backdrop of prominent industrial establishments offers a distinctive urban charm. The gravel path is well-maintained, making it suitable for walkers of all levels. Walking under the newly constructed road bridge added an element of modern infrastructure to the journey, enhancing the urban exploration feel.

Unlike typical walkways that traverse lush forests or coastal areas, the Puhinui Stream Walkway presents an industrial-urban setting that is both intriguing and refreshing. The contrast between the natural elements of the stream and the surrounding industrial environment provides a unique perspective on Auckland's diverse landscapes.

For those seeking a different kind of walking experience, the Puhinui Stream Walkway is a hidden gem worth exploring. Its distinctive urban-industrial scenery offers a refreshing departure from conventional nature walks. We highly recommend visiting this walkway to appreciate a unique facet of Auckland's environment.

I ended up at De Havilland Reserve kind of by accident, really. I was waiting for a takeaway order nearby and had some time to kill, so I thought I’d stretch my legs and go for a walk. I’d never been there before, but I’m glad I checked it out—turned out to be a surprisingly peaceful little spot.

The reserve is tucked away in the Goodwood Heights area, and even though it’s not a massive park, it’s got a really chill vibe. There’s a proper footpath that loops through the grassy area, which makes it easy for walking, jogging, or even pushing a pram if you’ve got kids in tow. I saw a couple of people riding scooters too, so it’s definitely family-friendly.

One thing I noticed right away is how quiet it was. You can still hear a bit of traffic in the distance, but for the most part, it’s just birds chirping and the odd rustle of trees. There are a few large trees that provide some good shade, and a couple of benches dotted around, which is perfect if you just want to sit and relax for a bit. I sat on one near the middle of the reserve and just people-watched for a few minutes—really peaceful.

What caught me off guard was the ducks! There were a few just waddling around near the grass and they actually came up pretty close to me. I wasn’t expecting that at all, but it was kinda funny. They clearly weren’t shy—probably used to people feeding them even though you’re not really supposed to. Still, it added a bit of charm to the whole walk.

The park seems to be well-maintained—no litter, grass was freshly mowed, and it generally looked tidy. There’s even a drinking fountain, which is always a nice touch if you’re walking or biking through on a hot day.

It’s also in a handy location. If you’ve got more time to spare, you could walk to Fairchild Avenue Reserve or even head over to Rainbow’s End or the Due Drop Events Centre, which are just a few minutes away by car. The whole area seems to have a good mix of green space and urban spots.

Overall, I wouldn’t say De Havilland Reserve is a destination park you’d plan a whole day around, but if you’re in the area—grabbing food, visiting family, or just passing through—it’s a great little place to relax, go for a walk, or let the kids run around. Quiet, clean, and just enough nature to give you a break from the hustle.

Would definitely pop back in next time I’m nearby.

Upper Nihotupu is one of the Auckland council's important water supply reservoirs. It is an amazing technological marvel considering the times (1920s) and the human visionary that demonstrate the excellent skills in forecasting decades ahead water supply needs of the ever-increasing city's population. Reservoir is built with a double curvature concrete dam across the Nihotupu stream, completed in 1923. The Nihotupu Dam is about 30m tall and store over 2.2 giga litres of water.

Turning halfway from Auckland-Piha main road you reach the adjoining small car park and do a walk about 5km on a well-maintained track by the Auckland Watercare services. Generally considered an easy route, it takes about an hour to complete one way. This is a popular trail for birding, hiking, and running. Starting though a beautiful native bush before joining a gravel road, this track is decorated with a couple of small waterfalls.  A further 10-minute walk will take you to a picnic area where you can see the 6.5km narrow gauge old tramline which carted the construction material to the base of the Nihotupu Dam in the early last century. Currently it functions as the maintenance line for the main water pipe that carries water to the Titirangi filtration plant. It was also the track used to run the famous 'Rainforest Express' which operated up until 2014.

The area has been extensively planted in natives, and there's plenty of wildlife making the most of the lake - even a cormorant.
But there's also plenty of rubble and rusted iron, and although they could have put in a walkway to the adjacent wetlands under the road, instead there's a barbed wire fence.
And in case you're thinking of sitting there in the sunset, feeding the ducks, the ducks are afraid of humans and when you throw them bread it just reinforces their fear. (which is probably good for the ducks, because they wouldn't do well living off bread, for multiple reasons.)

Upper Nihotupu reservoir track runs along one of the Auckland council's important water supply reservoirs in the Waitakere ranges.  Turning halfway from Auckland-Piha main road, you reach the adjoining small car park and do the walk about 5km on a well-maintained track by the Auckland Watercare services.

Generally considered an easy route, suitable for the family, it takes about an hour to complete one way. Starting through a small wooden bridge in a beautiful native bush, this track is decorated with a couple of small waterfalls along the way, particularly rich in the rainy season. After reaching the dam site, a further 10-minute walk plus number of steps will take you to the bottom of the concrete dam. There is a picnic area where you can see the beginning of a 6.5km narrow gauge old tramline which carted the construction material to the base of the Nihotupu Dam in the early last century. Currently it functions as the maintenance line for the main water pipe that carries water to the Titirangi filtration plant. It was also the track used to run the famous 'Rainforest Express' which operated up until 2014.

Manukau City's route extends over twice the distance of the North Shore City Coastal Walk, opened in November as part of Te Araroa. It crosses the Manukau Harbour on the old Mangere Bridge, follows the Mangere Gateway Heritage route along Kiwi Esplanade to Ambury Regional Park, then depending on timing goes around the recently restored edge of the Manukau Harbour beside the Mangere Wastewater Treatment Plant - or alternatively around Wallace, Creamery, Greenwood, Oruarangi and Ascot Roads - to the Otuataua Stonefields. It follows Ihumatao Road east, to George Bolt Memorial Drive past the Auckland International Airport, and onto Puhinui Road. It uses Prices Road to reach Puhinui Reserve, then follows the Puhinui Stream 12 kilometres to the City Centre.

From the City Centre it connects to Totara Park then heads south along Redoubt Road, connecting if possible through private land to Brownhill Road, right into Whitford Park Road, right into Brookby Road, left into Kimpton's Road, then follows an unformed paper road into Clevedon Scenic Reserve. A route may need to be negotiated on private land if this paper road is impassable, and Te Araroa volunteers have talked to private property owners about possibilities in this area. It follows existing walking tracks to the summit lookout, then out through the reserve's main entrance and into Clevedon. From there it follows the Clevedon-Kawakawa Road east over the Wairoa River, up McNicol Road past the McNicol Homestead, then follows the Wairoa River into the Wairoa Gorge, along a paper road and into the Hunua Ranges Regional Park.

This walkway wanders alongside the Manukau Harbour coastline, exploring the waterfront of Māngere Bridge township, before ending on the borders of Ambury Regional Park.

From Ambury Park, you can link up with the Watercare Coastal Walkway and continue on to the Ōtuataua Stonefields, along the Māngere Ihumātao foreshore.

The area is rich in history and natural beauty. Along the way, you will see evidence of Auckland's volcanic past, as well as countless native and migratory birds. You will also pass by New Zealand's biggest coastal marine restoration project.

I researched all the greenhouses on offer in NZ, looked carefully at the sites available on my property and thought long and hard about whether to go glass or twin wall poly.  I finally decided to go with the Trulux Maxi model on the grounds it met all my preferences and placed the order in early August 2015.

The project is now complete (early September) and I can honestly say it was a lot of fun and an extraordinarily positive experience. Apart from the concrete base (which a local builder installed) I assembled and constructed the entire greenhouse single handed.    Best of all I now have a valuable, attractive and very functional green house to hone my gardening skills in over many years ahead.

The design and manufacturing quality of the product is absolutely top notch - even down to the protective packaging it comes in.   The aluminium extrusions are precision formed and cut, the simple integral hex head bolt and nut system that locks the whole structure together is a work of genius and the glass is all chamfered and smoothed so it is safe and easy to handle.

When I first saw the size of the glass roof panels I had second thoughts about completing the job on my own.  I had visions of standing on ladders and manoeuvring 1.8 m long panes of glass overhead. Not ideal at my age.   I even thought about asking a professional glazier to give me a hand.  Come the day to install the glass panes I discovered you just stood on the ground and slid them up the pre-formed grooves in the roof bars until they dropped into place .... too easy!

Being a very average DIYer  I thought the manual could be a bit more descriptive.   I found it helpful to read right through the next stage of the project the night before. On the other hand the entire construction system is very forgiving and mistakes only ever take a couple of steps backward to fix.  Furthermore, Trulux operates an amazing 24 hour help desk known as Clint.    No problem is too small for Clint.

This weekend we had a Greenhouse warming party to celebrate the completion of the project.  It was a chilly 10 degrees outside at 6 on Saturday afternoon but with 20 of us crammed in the greenhouse it was warm enough for the automatic vents to open.  Brilliant.

Any regrets??? Yes I already miss the lovely old persimmon tree I had to remove to make way for the Maxi.  I am consoled by the thought of planting another persimmon very shortly and enjoying its fruits in a year or two.  In the meantime I take great satisfaction from having built such a beautiful and functional greenhouse.  Thanks Trulux.

The waterfall itself is stunning—a cascading beauty that feels like it’s been lifted straight out of a fairy tale (no wonder it’s called Fairy Falls!).

The climb back up is a bit of a challenge, especially because of the many stairs, but it’s absolutely doable even with young kids. We just took lots of little breaks, had some snacks, and enjoyed the forest vibes on the way back.
The walk is around 3.5 km return, and it’s a perfect day trip being just about 30–40 minutes from central Auckland.

The Fairy Falls Trailhead offers a rewarding experience, with a walk of less than 30 minutes to reach the breathtaking waterfall. The return journey is a bit longer, but it's a fantastic opportunity to boost your health and energy levels through physical activity. It's a great idea to fuel up with a full meal beforehand to make the most of your hike.

This is a pretty reserve tucked away amongst residential properties. Wide paths throughout the reserve connect the neighbourhood, and provide a safe route for the local children to walk to May Road Prmary School. The large number of plants and trees along the edge of the pond and around the reserve have created a great habitat for wildlife (particularly pūkeko and ducks) and improved the stormwater quality downstream. You can get good views of the pond and wildlife from the lookout platform. Access the reserve from between numbers 39 and 43, and 57 and 59 Freeland Avenue. You can also access from opposite number 21 Balfron Avenue and via a walkway between numbers 24 and 26 Kallu Crescent. Picnic tables and seating are inside the reserve. You will need to park on the road. You can also cross Freeland Avenue at the bottom of the reserve to access the playground at Turner Reserve.

Functionality: Beyond its aesthetic appeal, the fountain serves a practical purpose as a gathering spot for locals and tourists alike. Whether it's a leisurely afternoon stroll or a romantic evening rendezvous, the fountain provides a picturesque backdrop for memorable moments.

Legacy: Named in honor of John Park, a beloved community leader known for his dedication to public service, the fountain stands as a testament to his enduring legacy. It symbolizes the enduring spirit of unity and compassion that he embodied.

In conclusion, the John Park Memorial Fountain is more than just a landmark—it's a symbol of serenity, elegance, and the enduring power of community. Highlights:
🌿 Magical vibes – The sunlight filtering through the ancient trees was straight out of a fairy tale.
🚶 Perfect length – Took us about 1.5 hours at a relaxed pace, with plenty of photo stops.
💦 Small cascades – The little waterfalls along the way added such a serene touch.

Only note: Wear good shoes (some parts can be muddy after rain), and don’t forget insect repellent!

Highly recommend for nature lovers, couples, or friends wanting a rejuvenating escape. We left feeling so refreshed—will definitely be back!

Heron Park is one of those places that quietly impresses you the more you explore it. Tucked away in Waterview, this park offers a perfect mix of wide open fields, bushy trails, and elevated views that make it ideal for families, walkers, and nature lovers alike.

The walking paths are well laid out, with gentle slopes and scenic spots that let you soak in the beauty of the area. There’s a real sense of community here — from joggers and dog walkers to parents with kids enjoying the playground or riding bikes.

The views from the top of the park are a highlight, especially at sunset, with glimpses of the city and harbour. The playground is modern and fun, and there's enough space for a good game of soccer or a picnic under the trees.

It’s peaceful, well-maintained, and feels like a sanctuary in the middle of suburbia. If you’re ever in the area or looking for a new weekend walk spot, Heron Park is definitely worth checking out.

The Te Auaunga  / Oakley creek area is one of the largest and most developed ecosystems in the urban Auckland area.

There are developed walking and shared bike/walking paths throughout.

The western side of Great North Rd includes the skatepark, playground, pump track, and a pathway along the waterfront through Howlett Reserve.

The eastern side of Great North Rd includes numerous walking paths, community gardens, it neighbors onto the unitec campus grounds.

There is a water hole at the Oakley creek waterfall site which is a popular diving site (at your own risk - caution advised).

The local community collaborate on a range of ecology projects and the area is well kept.

There are historic volcanic rock walls which is a nod to the geological history of the area.

You could spend days exploring this area and still find new things to see and new personalities of the area.

A Panoramic Gem
Mount Eden is a must-visit destination in Auckland, offering breathtaking 360-degree views of the city. This dormant volcano is a popular spot for both locals and tourists.

Highlights
1. *Panoramic views*: Enjoy stunning views of Auckland's skyline, including the iconic Sky Tower.
2. *Hike to the summit*: A moderate hike takes you to the top, where the views are simply spectacular.
3. *Historic significance*: Mount Eden is a culturally significant site, with evidence of Maori settlement dating back centuries.

Tips
1. *Wear comfortable shoes*: The hike can be steep in some areas, so wear shoes that are suitable for walking.
2. *Bring water and snacks*: There are limited facilities at the summit, so come prepared.
3. *Visit at sunset*: The views are particularly stunning during sunset.

Worth It
The hike may require some effort, but the views from the summit are well worth it. On a clear day, you can see the entire city, including the harbor and surrounding landscape.

If you're looking for a spot to take in the sights and sounds of Auckland, Mount Eden is a must-visit destination.

Visiting Mount Eden in Auckland is an exhilarating experience. As you ascend the volcanic cone, the panoramic views of the city and its shimmering harbor take your breath away. The lush green landscape and the vibrant sky create a serene backdrop, inviting reflection and peace. Standing at the summit, you feel a sense of accomplishment and connection to nature. The cool breeze and the distant sounds of the city remind you of life's hustle, yet here, you find tranquility. Each moment spent at Mount Eden leaves you rejuvenated, inspired, and grateful for the beauty that surrounds you.

If you would come to Auckland, and you miss this place, I would say you have missed the best part of Auckland. You can reach this place by walking from CBD, or take a taxi or Didi. Udy's Reserve was named after my Great-great-grandmothers family.

My Great-great-grandmother Mary Udy came to NZ  from Cornwall with her parents George & Jane Udy and her 6 siblings in 1859 on the sailing ship NIMROD.

Mary married Thomas Wakelin on 24th August 1865 at Eden Grove. Shortly afterwards they moved north to Whangarei and then to Kamo where Thomas started several businesses.
Wakelin Street in Kamo is named after him.

Access Te Henga walkway from Constable rd. This walk is quite a hike. Is not suitable for the elderly or those who aren't particularly fit. Quite a bit of stairs to go down at first and very steep, literally almost vertical. Some parts of track are not the easiest to walk, but aren't impossible. Track gets narrow for a little bit and then is open as. Beautiful views, nature all around you and open skies. Then there's a mountain climb, but I swear the view at the top is worth every second of the climb. So beautiful. You can see the coastline and vast open ocean, it's breathtaking 😍 Love the West coast 💙

There is also a waterfall (see last image) you can see on the right side from the mountain top. We didn't get to go and see it as the track was closed, but it looked to be another hour and a half - 2 hours away (obvs via foot).

I would definitely only recommend the Te Henga walkway for those with a moderate to advanced level of fitness. This track is not suitable for prams.

The track starts out with a series of stairs, which are quite steep in places and will be muddy after rain. You descend the stairs when starting out, which means an intense climb on the return leg.
The track continues on through farmland and up a bit of a 'scramble' where the real coastal walk begins.
The track itself is quite  rugged and not maintained. During winter it is common for parts of the track to wash out and you need to carefully climb across parts.
Sunblock is absolutely recommended as the coastal track is not in the shade.

For your efforts, you are rewarded with beautiful West Coast views and a decent cardio workout.

A Hidden Gem in Auckland – Meola Reef Rocks!

Meola Reef is one of those places that feels like a well-kept local secret. Whether you're going for a peaceful walk, bringing your furry friend to the dog park, or just taking in the views of the Waitematā Harbour, this spot has something special.

The volcanic rock formations are fascinating and give the place a raw, natural feel you won’t find in many city parks. The walking track is flat and easy to navigate, perfect for a casual stroll or a morning jog. The open field is great for families, and the off-leash dog area is a total hit with our pup – loads of space to run, sniff, and make new four-legged friends.

You also get a unique vantage point of Auckland’s skyline from the end of the reef. If you're into photography or just love a good sunset, it’s absolutely worth the visit.

It’s not flashy – no playgrounds or cafes – but what it offers is a slice of nature and calm that’s hard to come by in a busy city. Meola Reef is a reminder that sometimes the simplest places can be the most refreshing.

New Zealand's Parliament met in Auckland, which was then the capital city, from its first sitting in 1854 until its permanent move to Wellington in 1865 (apart from one session in 1862). The members of the inaugural Parliament complained about the basic facilities of the building on Constitution Hill, close to the present-day University of Auckland.

It was little more than a bare shell and became known as the 'Shedifice'. The wind whistled through the walls, and the roof leaked. There was no clock, division bell or strongroom to protect documents. Initially there was nowhere to get food or drink, and not even a toilet. Parliamentarians' working environment would be far more comfortable following the shift to Wellington.

This view of Parliament Buildings (far left) and St Paul's, above Mechanics Bay, is from Parnell Rise. Andrew Robertson, Auckland from Parnell, 1859.

Great reserve for a beautiful evening walk. We started from Onetaunga road entrance, walked through the reserve. On the way back we took a diversion to Kendall bay.

Great views throughout the walk with seats/benches placed at strategic viewpoints. You'll encounter birds such as tui, fantail etc.. Tracks are good though not much manmade and marked. It's kind of a clearing through the tree roots and hence can get slippery if wet.

Though it's an easy walk, average fitness is required as there are a few cliff areas which will connect to the Chelsea Heritage park. If you've more time, you can combine this with the Chatswood reseve which will take an hour extra.

Overall a pleasant experience and a must do in Auckland, especially if you love reserve walking.

Le Roy's Bush Reserve is one of the very popular tramping bushes in the North Shore of Auckland. You can either enter from Hinemoa Street in Hibury or from the Little Shoal Bay side and the loop track runs for about 3.5km. Generally considered an easy route, it takes an average one and a half to two hours to complete the loop leisurely. This is a very popular bush for bird watching, running, and walking. Dogs are allowed but must be on a leash. It has a nice canopy of trees with lots of interesting flora and fauna. It contains lowland forest with significant presence of kauri-tanekaha, broadleaved, and pohutukawa with wetland associations to the nearby estuary.  The Shoal Bay Stream is habitat for indigenous fish including inanga, banded kokopu, longfin eel and shortfin eel.

Le Roy's Bush was originally purchased by Edward Le Roy in 1918. He established three ponds where he grew water lilies and kept goldfish. After his death the reserve was purchased by a public subscription organized by the North Shore Branch of the Forest and Bird Society and has since been extended from the original block by addition of further purchases of bush-clad back yards. Now the Bush spreads into about 12 hectares in extent where it joins the Little Shoal Bay Reserve (7.5 hectares) and Lutmers Reserve (2.6 hectares) near Wilding Ave in Northcote.

text: I enjoyed seeing the beautiful Rainbow Warrior Memorial mosaic while walking around the harbour in Auckland. It helped remind me of the importance to protect our environment from the stupidity of man. It is too bad that history repeats itself over and over. I fear that man will eventually will bring our fragile living environment to the point where of our own demise and cause the extinction of the human race.

At Marden Wharf in July 1985 the Rainbow Warrior, flagship for Greenpeace, was bombed and sunk by agents of the French Government killing photographer Fernando Pereira. The ship was about to sail into the Pacific in peaceful protest against French nuclear testing. Public outrage and continuing pressure led France to stop the bomb tests after 1995 leaving irreparable damage at Moruroa.
Today the Rainbow Warrior Il inspires people everywhere as she continues to campaign around the globe 'bearing witness' against nuclear weapons and all other destructive environmental practices.
'You can't sink a rainbow.  Mosaic by dan Morrison from a design by Vicki Worthington, assisted by Claudia Pond Eyley. With thanks to Ports of Auckland and the Peace and Disarmament Education Trust. Completed for the 30" annt versary of Greenpeace September 2001.

North Head (Maungauika) in Devonport is a fantastic spot for a family outing or a local adventure. The dramatic grassy slopes offer sweeping views of Rangitoto, the city skyline, and the Hauraki Gulf, and the historic World War II tunnels and bunkers add an intriguing twist.

One of the most joyful local pastimes? Sliding down the lush grass banks on a piece of cardboard.
It’s a simple pleasure—kids (and adults!) run up the slope, sit on their cardboard, and zoom down the hill with laughter and exhilaration  . Whether you're there at golden hour or midday, grabbing a piece of cardboard from home (or sometimes recycled from nearby cafés) ensures hours of spontaneous fun.

Past the grassy slides, don’t miss exploring the historic tunnels, disappearing guns, and coastal bunkers. The contrast of fun and history makes it a memorable outing—picnic on the grass, then duck into the atmospheric caverns, torch in hand.

In short:

Eksdale reserve is located between Glenfield and Birkdale suburbs in the North Shore region of greater Auckland. I would say this reserve is the pair of lungs of Glenfield and Birkdale, as the lush green patch right in the centre of this suburban precinct cleaning emissions of the surrounding area. The reserve extends to about 74ha and is one of the most unique urban eco systems in the Auckland ecological landscape. It also  has connections to the few remaining salt water mixed swamps in Auckland.

There are multiple walking tracks in this reserve which you can access from a couple of points on Glenfield Rd, Eksdale Rd, Lauderdale Rd, Beach Haven Rd, Seaview Rd, Brunton place etc., where street parking is widely available. These easy, shady bush walking tracks are perfectly suitable for anyone, particularly on sweltering summer days. In the winter, parts of the tracks get muddy, but most parts are gravel laid and well maintained so it is not as bad. Mountain biking and dogs on leash allowed.

This native bush thrives with nikau palms, young kauri trees and ponga tree ferns and the Kaipatiki Stream runs along this reserve. In the spring or after a rain, you can see a little waterfall if you access the reserve from Eksdale side.

The park became well known for its rose gardens and its memorial drinking fountain. The fountain was dedicated to the memory of the Collins family, which was one of Takapuna’s oldest families. John and Sarah Collins moved to Takapuna from Tuakau in 1896. John worked as the head gardener of the Brett Estate on Killarney Street, while Sarah ran a successful tuck shop out of their house on Anzac Street opposite the school.

A stone birdbath in the centre of the garden was created by Auckland sculptor John Edgar, who made similar artworks for other parks in the city shortly after the supercity was created in 2010.

The Takapuna Fossil Forest is a geographical feature located along the coastline between Takapuna Beach and Thorne Beach in Auckland, New Zealand. It consists of a series of basalt rock formations, which are the result of lava flows through an ancient forest.

It is believed to be New Zealand's most well-preserved fossil forest in NZ.

Explore the fossil forest while walking the coastal walkway between the northern end of Takapuna Beach and Milford.

If you go at low tide, the remains of a petrified Kauri tree (New Zealand native) forest.

About 100,000 years ago the sea level was much lower and kauri, pohutukawa, and mixed broadleaf trees covered the coast. Around this time, the volcano that created Lake Pupuke erupted for the last time, covering the forest in lava.

The lava covered the trees, turned them into flaming torches. The trees that were not incinerated immediately rotted within the cooling lava, which eventually turned into a hard basalt shell. At low tide, the remnants of 500 tree stumps and branches can be seen on the reef. Perfectly formed hollow imprints of the trunks detailing bark and leaves are visible, some lying horizontal in the rock face and others standing upright. One of these, a 1.6-metre-diameter, 3-metre-deep kauri trunk, has been covered by metal grating for safety and is often mistaken for a well.

The extensive area now known as Woodhill Forest is an important part of the cultural landscape of Ngāti Whātua o Kaipara. Many ancestral names (like Te Kēti, Kuwakatai, Waionui, Korekore and Ōkiritoto) were used for different areas and features, but the land became generally known as Woodhill when it passed into Crown ownership to be developed as forest.

Today, the land under the forest is privately owned and managed by Ngā Maunga Whakahii o Kaipara after a 2013 Treaty of Waitangi settlement.

The Riverhead Walkway, nestled within the picturesque Riverside Forest in Auckland, is a lovely spot for outdoor enthusiasts. This scenic walkway offers a tranquil escape from the hustle and bustle of city life, immersing visitors in the sights and sounds of nature.

However, please note that the walkway is less maintained than other tracks in the area. The path is narrow throughout the entire track, requiring careful walking. Additionally, be aware that:

- Bicyclists also share the same track, so keep an ear out for approaching riders.
- Spikes from plants along the track can be hazardous, so watch your step and wear protective clothing.
- There are no designated picnic spots along the way, so plan accordingly.

Before embarking on your walk, be sure to:

- Bring plenty of water to stay hydrated
- Wear full clothing, including comfortable walking shoes and protective gear (as the track can be uneven and rough in some areas)

While the Riverhead Walkway requires some caution and maintenance, it's still a great spot for nature lovers, walkers, and anyone seeking a peaceful escape from the city. So pack your water, wear comfortable shoes, and immerse yourself in the beauty of Riverside Forest.

Recommended for: Nature lovers, walkers, and anyone seeking a peaceful escape from the city.

We stayed in their eco glamping unit. What an experience! Read further if you want a (really) comprehensive review.

The unit is an old caravan which has been converted into a quaint little home for two. The caravan opens out onto a spacious deck with a table and two chairs, with beautiful forest views and a stunning sky of stars at night. The spa bath and outdoor shower are on the deck around a corner, and one has total privacy. The sounds of nature fill the space, and one feels instantly relaxed.

One can take a walk around the site and explore, or along one of the forest walk routes. There is also a forest bath for guests to use, in which you can relax and bath surrounded by nature.

Amenities were perfectly supplied and went over and above: we were welcomed with a basket filled with goodies + a handwritten note. The room was equipped with basics (eggs, milk, fruit juice, butter, jam, salt & pepper and more) and we were greeted with freshly baked bread in the mornings which was amazing! The dinners served were great, and really had that home cooked taste, which we loved. The desserts were fantastic!

That being said, we were fully fed for breakfast and dinner. For lunch, you’re a short drive from Albany, the local town. You can pop into town for a meal, or bring back some supplies and cook for yourself. The cooking process was fun - a BBQ on the deck just outside the caravan door and all the pots, pans and other utensils you may need around the corner from the caravan. The unit was also equipped with robes, towels, slippers and blankets, which made us feel really cozy and comfy!

We loved the retro vibe of the converted caravan - it’s very clear that the hosts have wonderful attention to detail and put intentional care into it. The whole place is super eco-friendly, which means that the loo is a compost one! A fun experience for those of us accustomed to regular hotel bathrooms.

The hosts clearly understand the balance between giving guests their privacy and making guests feel welcome. Really friendly, super accommodating, but give you your space as well.

One thing about the wifi was that it did not reach the caravan, and there’s very little to no cellular signal at all inside of it. One can walk a few metres to the canopy (a little venue perfect for an intimate wedding) for wifi, but the wifi is not fast at all. If you’re someone who needs to stay available via the internet, you should probably make alternative plans to be able to connect during your stay. If you’re like us, though, and really need an escape from your phones and devices, the no wifi thing may be a blessing in disguise! We really feel that the digital detox added to how rejuvenated we felt after the stay. Although we had no wifi, the caravan has board games which we had fun with, and there’s a little book inside the caravan with the history of the place, as well as little handbooks about the history of the local town, natural sites and so on, which we really enjoyed reading through!

All in all, this stay cannot be faulted at all, and was the perfect reset. As avid travellers with high standards, this place managed to totally surpass our expectations. Dave and Barb, you have outdone yourself! Thank you so much.

The Gauntlet is a rugged coastal passage named after the infamous seafarer Murray, who bravely charted this route with nothing but a questionable sense of timing and a dinghy that always sailed at half mast. Locals say you’re not truly from the Shore until you’ve braved Murray’s Gauntlet and lost a jandal to the tide. Bring snacks. And a will

It really is a challenging yet rewarding coastal traverse.

Murray’s Gauntlet isn’t for the faint-hearted — and that’s exactly why it’s one of the most memorable challenges I’ve ever experienced.

From the moment you start, it’s clear this isn’t your average obstacle course (or game/experience — depending on what it is). Murray has designed something that tests not just your strength and endurance, but your focus, adaptability, and mental toughness. Every section of the gauntlet demands a different skillset, and just when you think you’ve got the rhythm, it throws in a twist that knocks you off balance — literally and figuratively.

What sets Murray’s Gauntlet apart is the attention to detail. The difficulty is high, yes, but never unfair. Every failure teaches you something. Every success feels earned. And when you finally make it through, you don’t just feel relief — you feel transformation. You’ve proven something to yourself.

Whether you’re a seasoned competitor or just someone looking for a next-level challenge, Murray’s Gauntlet is unforgettable. You’ll walk away sore, exhausted, and absolutely hooked.

The campground was full, the sign said. I spoke to the host, Roy, and he said people hadn't turned up and there was plenty of space if I wanted to stay. No sooner had I replied, thank you, this woman came bustling to the door of their rig, Mrs Moanie Roy? and said "I've just spoke to the council and they are going to close the campground because it's too wet." I responded that it wasn't too wet now. But the ground is, she replied, as I am standing on dry ground. "And the toilets are going to stop working, so no-one will be able to use those."  How she had that premonition, who knows.
Poor Roy. He seemed such a nice friendly man.
I said, have a nice day and walked back to where I'd parked outside the gate.  The campground had lots of dry camping spots, and the toilets were working.  I decided to camp at the other secluded area away from the campground and booked online accordingly to find there were 7 spaces for that night and 19 spaces available for the following night.
Auckland Council.  I would change your hosts if I were you.
I have given a 1 star rating for Moanie. However, I would give a 4 star for Roy, the park, toilet blocks, and the beach.
